mcqs.q: The essential armamentarium for a local anaesthetic injection is the:
opts: Cotton rolls and a mouth mirror
mcqs.explain: Essentials are the syringe, needle and cartridge; topical antiseptic, gauze, topical anaesthetic, applicators and a hemostat are 'additional'.

mcqs.q: The harpoon of an aspirating syringe functions to:
opts: Engage the rubber stopper so aspiration can be performed
Hold the needle to the hub
mcqs.explain: The harpoon on the piston engages the rubber stopper; negative pressure on the thumb ring then draws blood back if the needle is intravascular.

mcqs.q: Aspiration before injecting is performed to:
opts: Minimise the risk of an intravascular injection
mcqs.explain: Aspiration checks whether the needle tip is inside a blood vessel, minimising the risk of an intravascular injection.

mcqs.q: Regarding needle gauge:
opts: A smaller gauge number means a wider lumen (30G is narrower than 25G)
A smaller gauge number means a narrower lumen
Gauge refers to the needle length
All dental needles have the same gauge
mcqs.explain: Gauge is the lumen diameter; the smaller the number, the wider the lumen — so 30G has a narrower lumen than 25G.

mcqs.q: The most commonly used dental needles are:
mcqs.explain: The 30-gauge short and 27-gauge long needles are most commonly used in dentistry.

mcqs.q: A standard dental cartridge contains approximately:
mcqs.explain: The glass cartridge (carpule) holds about 1.8 mL of local anaesthetic solution.

mcqs.q: A dental cartridge should NOT be used if its:
opts: Rubber stopper protrudes beyond the glass margin
Stopper is slightly indented from the margin
mcqs.explain: In an intact cartridge the stopper is slightly indented; a stopper extruded beyond the glass margin indicates a problem — discard it.

mcqs.q: On the ASA physical status scale, an ASA I patient is:
opts: A patient with severe systemic disease
mcqs.explain: ASA I = normal healthy; II mild–moderate disease; III severe (limits activity); IV constant threat to life; V moribund; VI brain-dead.

mcqs.q: From which ASA class is elective dental care generally contraindicated?
mcqs.explain: Elective care is contraindicated from ASA IV (only non-invasive emergency care, with consultation/hospitalisation as needed).

mcqs.q: In a local anaesthetic skin sensitivity test, a positive reaction means:
opts: The patient is allergic — use a different drug
mcqs.explain: An LA wheal and a saline control are compared at 5 minutes; a positive (allergic) reaction means another drug must be used.

mcqs.q: A disposable needle should be changed after approximately:
mcqs.explain: Sharpness diminishes with use; the needle should be changed after about 3 tissue penetrations to keep insertion atraumatic.

mcqs.q: The ideal temperature of the local anaesthetic solution at injection is:
opts: Body temperature heated in hot water
mcqs.explain: The solution should be at room temperature (18–22 °C); too cold or too hot causes discomfort. Warm a cold cartridge in the hand for 5–7 min.

mcqs.q: The recommended patient position for injection, to avoid fainting, is:
opts: Supine, with the head/heart level and feet slightly elevated
mcqs.explain: The supine position (head and heart parallel to the floor, feet slightly elevated) helps prevent vasodepressor syncope (the common faint).

mcqs.q: Topical anaesthetic should remain in contact with the mucosa for at least:
mcqs.explain: Topical anaesthetic should stay in contact with the mucosa for at least 2 minutes to be effective at the penetration site.

mcqs.q: When communicating before injection, the operator should:
opts: Avoid the words 'pain' and 'hurt' (even in reassurance)
Repeat 'it will not hurt' several times
mcqs.explain: Avoid 'pain'/'hurt'; saying 'it will not hurt' backfires because the patient hears only 'hurt'. Keep the syringe out of sight, especially with children.

mcqs.q: Just before needle insertion, the tissue should be:
mcqs.explain: Taut tissue lets the sharp needle penetrate easily; loose tissue is pushed and torn, causing more discomfort and post-op soreness.

mcqs.q: The recommended syringe grip giving the best control is:
mcqs.explain: A palm-up grip with finger/wrist support gives better control; palm-down gives poor control and is not recommended.

mcqs.q: 'Slow' deposition of local anaesthetic is defined as:
opts: 1 mL in not less than 60 seconds
mcqs.explain: Slow injection (1 mL in ≥60 s) avoids tissue ballooning/tearing, reduces post-op pain and slows systemic absorption.

mcqs.q: Large air bubbles must be expelled from the cartridge because they risk:
opts: Air injection into a vein or tissues (emphysema)
mcqs.explain: Large air bubbles should be eliminated to avoid injecting air into a vein or soft tissue (emphysema); very small volumes are harmless.

mcqs.q: The needle tip should NEVER be introduced into a foramen because it may cause:
mcqs.explain: Entering a foramen risks damaging vessels and nerves, causing haematoma, paraesthesia and prolonged anaesthesia.

mcqs.q: During injection near bone, the needle bevel should be:
opts: Directed toward the bone, without scrubbing the periosteum
Kept fully buried in the periosteum
mcqs.explain: Direct the bevel toward bone and avoid scrubbing the periosteum with the tip, which is very painful.

mcqs.q: Which is a recognised method of achieving local anaesthesia?
opts: Infiltration, field block and nerve block
mcqs.explain: Methods of LA include topical, infiltration, field block and nerve block.

mcqs.q: An advantage of a nerve block over infiltration is that it:
opts: Gives more profound, longer anaesthesia with fewer punctures and is usable near infection
Causes local ischaemia of the surgical field
mcqs.explain: Nerve blocks are more profound and longer, need fewer punctures and less drug, can be used near infection without spreading it, and avoid local ischaemia.

mcqs.q: Additional (non-essential) armamentarium includes the:
mcqs.explain: Additional armamentarium: topical antiseptic, cotton/gauze, topical anaesthetic, applicator sticks and a hemostat.

mcqs.q: The aspirating dental syringe is best described as:
opts: A breech-loading, metallic, reusable (after sterilisation) syringe
A disposable plastic syringe used once
A glass syringe that cannot aspirate
mcqs.explain: It is a breech-loading, metallic (chrome-plated brass or stainless steel) aspirating syringe, reusable after sterilisation.

mcqs.q: The part of the cartridge the needle pierces to reach the solution is the:
mcqs.explain: The needle pierces the semipermeable diaphragm, which is held over the cartridge neck by the aluminium cap; the stopper at the other end receives the harpoon.

mcqs.q: Before injection the operator should establish a firm hand rest mainly to:
opts: Allow steady needle insertion without jerking
mcqs.explain: A firm hand rest enables steady, controlled needle insertion without undue jerking of the hand.

mcqs.q: Free flow of solution is checked before injection by:
opts: Expelling a few drops after loading the cartridge
mcqs.explain: After loading, a few drops are expelled to confirm the solution flows freely through the needle.

mcqs.q: The final step after completing the injection is to:
opts: Observe the patient and record the injection in the chart
Immediately reuse the same needle on the next site
mcqs.explain: After slow withdrawal and recapping, observe the patient and record the injection (drug, dose, site) in the patient's chart.

saqs.q: List the essential and additional LA armamentarium.
saqs.a: Essential: syringe, needle, cartridge. Additional: topical antiseptic, cotton/gauze, topical anaesthetic, applicator sticks, hemostat.
Gauge = lumen diameter; the smaller the number the wider the lumen (30G narrower than 25G); common are 30G short and 27G long. Length (hub→tip): long ≈32 mm, short ≈20 mm.

saqs.q: Describe the parts of a dental cartridge.
saqs.a: A glass cylinder of ~1.8 mL with a rubber stopper (receives the harpoon), an aluminium cap, and a diaphragm (semipermeable membrane the needle pierces). Discard if the stopper protrudes.

saqs.q: Outline the ASA physical status classes I–VI.
saqs.a: I normal healthy; II mild–moderate systemic disease; III severe disease limiting activity; IV severe, constant threat to life; V moribund; VI brain-dead.

saqs.q: List the key steps of an atraumatic injection.
saqs.a: Sharp sterile needle, warm solution, check flow, supine position, dry tissue, antiseptic, topical (≥2 min), communicate, firm hand rest, taut tissue, insert, aspirate, inject slowly (1 mL ≥60 s), withdraw slowly, record.
Eliminate large air bubbles (emphysema risk); never enter a foramen (haematoma/paraesthesia); direct the bevel toward bone and don't scrub the periosteum.

saqs.q: List the advantages of a nerve block over infiltration.
saqs.a: More profound and longer, fewer needle punctures, usable near infection without spreading it, less drug volume (fewer complications), and no local ischaemia (less infection, less pain, faster healing).
